All right, I got some notes because I don't do this often. So my name is Raquel Chapman, and I'm running for chairperson mostly because I know how exactly it feels to have a child who feels they're not welcomed. So, a little background. Four years ago, my husband and I made the decision to move our son from private school to our local, very small elementary school in

our neighborhood, which is only two miles from our house, instead of having to drive all the way into Leesburg every single day. Within his first few weeks of school, he was bullied by his classmates, and he was told directly that he was not welcomed in his new school because he was a different color. So, as any parent would, I went looking for help. Went right online to our favorite little spot, where they say the old people. I don't know if the young people like this anymore, but I went on Facebook and I

put in a post because I needed to know who I could talk to because I needed help. I was connected to several resources, including an introduction to MSAC. I walked into this committee as a mother with a fire in her chest and a desire to protect my child. What I found was something much larger than that. I found a community of families, students, and advocates navigating many of the same invisible barriers, not because resources did not

exist, but because too often families did not know where to look for them. That experience became the lens through which I understand MSAC's mission: to partner with Loudoun County Public Schools, parents, and the community to acknowledge and promote the needs of minority students while building a school system that is culturally and socially competent and positioned to provide fair and equitable learning experiences for all students. Those words are not abstract to me.

They describe exactly what my son needed on his first day at a new school, and exactly what too many of our children in this county are still waiting for. The most persistent barrier I've witnessed during my four years of service as an MSAC delegate is not always the absence of programs. It's the absence of knowledge about them. Families who understand how the system works often have an advantage over those families who are just equally committed. They just simply do not know what resources,

supports, or opportunities are available. Closing that information gap is one of the most direct ways we fulfill our mission of fair and equitable learning experiences for all students. Over the past four years, MSAC has equipped me personally with knowledge about school processes, resources, supports, and advocacy pathways that have strengthened my ability to advocate not only for my own child, but for other families navigating similar challenges.

I've become a resource for parents seeking guidance, helping connect them to information, supports, and opportunities they may not have known existed. That has become one of the most meaningful parts of my service, ensuring families feel informed, empowered, and less alone. My commitment to serving youth and families does not stop within the school system. I'm also a volunteer track and field coach for one of our local track teams in

the county, where I work closely with families, athletes with diverse backgrounds. In that role, I regularly help parents understand available resources, navigate opportunities, and advocate for their children's success both on and off the track. Whether in schools, sports, or the broader community, my approach has remained the same: build relationships, share information, and help families access the support they need to thrive.

What prepares me for this leadership role is not only my time on this committee. For over a decade, I've served in leadership positions across Maryland and Virginia healthcare systems as a regional laboratory consultant, supervisor, and manager. In those roles, I led diverse teams, managed complex systems across multiple facilities and states, drove measurable outcomes in high-stakes environments, and developed the organizational and interpersonal skills effective leadership demands. I know how to build consistence

across competing priorities, facilitate productive discussions, and hold institutions accountable to their stated commitments. Those skills translate directly to the chairperson role here, and they are skills this committee deserves in its leader. For two of my four years as delegate, I served as one of MSAC's representatives on the LCPS Equity Committee, where I worked at the systems level to advance equity initiatives and build relationships necessary to move meaningful change.

That experience deepened my conviction that MSAC is most effective when it operates as an active and trusted partner to LCPS, not just a symbolic one. While centering the voices of the families, our mission is designed to serve. My vision for MSAC as chairperson is anchored in our shared mission. I will strengthen partnerships between LCPS parents and the community by making those partnerships active, visible, and accountable.

I will prioritize culturally and socially competent outreach that reaches families who need MSAC the most and may not yet know we exist. I will work to ensure recommendations to the superintendent and school board are data-informed, actionable, and tied to measurable outcomes for minority students. Most importantly, I will continue working to close the information gap so families across Loudoun County understand not only what challenges exist, but

what resources and opportunities are available to help address them. Now, as my son prepares to enter middle school, I am more committed to this work than ever. What started as a mother advocating for her child has grown into a broader commitment to serving families throughout our community.I am asking for your vote because I'm ready to lead this committee. With lived experience, four years of institutional knowledge as a delegate, proven leadership experience, and a deeply personal commitment to
advancing equitable outcomes for every student we serve. Thank you.

can document, that we can stand on and honor and learn from as we continue to move forward in this work. PTA and the DEIEI efforts at my son's elementary and middle schools in the Potomac Fall Cluster for seven years now. I know what it's like to try to find ways to do the most good and the least harm. And in my career, I've had a chance to lead many nonprofits and boards, and so I have a lot of experience in strategic development, in management, in facilitation, in program implementation, and evaluation so that we can learn and grow. So I really

want to share now what matters most to me in this role, and that is partnership. And I know you all feel that strongly in your souls as well, because you come to MSAC repeatedly, and you have deep community relationships outside of MSAC, just as I do, just as you heard others do too, right? We are not just wearing one hat. We wear multiple hats, and we represent multiple constituencies, some that may be visible and some that may not be visible.

But they all make us who we are, and those collaborations really help us to strengthen this committee inside and across the county. I want to jump now into my three priorities. I want to continue first to strengthen the membership drive that we have launched this second half of the school year, and we really need to fill all of these tables next year. We need to get delegates here, we need to get

student delegates here, we need to get equity leads here, and we need to have a full room so that we can have a full conversation. Every school community deserves to have a voice at the table, and we also need stronger engagement from our delegates. I also want to explore how to make these meetings more accessible and think also about the economic constraints for traveling to a meeting like this as prices

continue to change, and how we might be able to support the folks who are in the room toTry to use an organizing tactic, a community organizing tactic, of actually coming together to break bread. And the snacks are great, but maybe there are ways that we can think about even doing more, just communing together in our meetings. Secondly, I want to

continue to build on the amazing work that you all do, have done, will continue to do. But that means we have to build a repository of resources, a toolkit that delegates can access regularly, early and often, can contribute to, can update, and make that really an opportunity for ensuring our delegates are informed, feel empowered, and are ready

for whatever question sort of comes up. And finally, and most importantly, and you've already heard this, I also think we have to prioritize understanding the real experiences of our students in Loudoun County, and that includes getting our real data. It means every time we get a presentation, we get the data that we need to have the analysis that we

must and are held through our mission to be conducting. It also means that we have to listen to what is happening. This weekend, I was informed of a high school student who stepped away from his desk to grab some hand sanitizer, and upon return, saw the N-word and a swastika drawn on his school paper.

May 2026. And so I just want to tell you that it's incidents like this that remind us that our work is not theoretical at all. It impacts whether our kids feel safe, whether they feel valued, and whether they feel like they belong. So we should continue to celebrate LCPS and MSAC's efforts across the district around DEIB, but we also have to be honest about the challenges that really do exist, even in a school district that is 60%

minority, but also one of the wealthiest counties in the country, where some of our students are still food insecure, they are housing insecure. outcomes will no longer face that. And so that their peers who aren't facing that will understand those struggles and be able to stand in solidarity with their peers. So, that is why I'm running for MSAC chair, and it really is about making sure that the part of our mission, the fair and equitable learning experience for all, is not just a conversation, but it's a practice, it's a policy, and it has outcomes.
